title: Distributional and multi-timescale error signals

The classical temporal-difference account writes the dopaminergic teaching signal as a single scalar error, δ=r+γV(s′)−V(s)\delta=r+\gamma V(s')-V(s). But the emerging physiological picture suggests that this scalar is best understood as an idealization of a structured population code. The basic RPE computation still appears to be shared across dopamine neurons: they retain a common subtractive response function, and the scalar TD formalism remains the right first approximation. Yet the neurons implementing that computation are not perfectly redundant copies of one another. Instead, different dopaminergic channels appear to instantiate different parameterizations of the error computation, allowing the basal ganglia to learn not only the mean of future return but aspects of its full distribution over both reward magnitude and reward time 1, 2, 3, 4.

The clearest evidence for a distributional reward code came from Dabney and colleagues, who showed that VTA dopamine neurons differ systematically in their reversal points and in the relative scaling of positive versus negative prediction errors. In other words, the population is not organized around one shared prediction with noise added on top; rather, individual neurons behave as though they are tilted toward more optimistic or more pessimistic slices of the return distribution. That is precisely the pattern expected if different dopamine channels converge toward different expectile-like estimates of future reward. Importantly, this result does not abolish the scalar RPE idea; it refines it. Each neuron still computes an error-like signal, but the population as a whole spans a family of asymmetric error channels whose aggregate activity can represent multimodal reward distributions that mean-based TD learning cannot recover 2, 5.

What physiological architecture could generate this distributional diversity? The safest answer is: not one mechanism, but several layered together. Part of the heterogeneity likely originates upstream of the dopamine neuron. Dopamine populations are projection-defined, receive different mixtures of sensory, motor, cognitive, and motivational inputs, and can therefore inherit different feature weightings from their afferent circuitry 6, 7. This point has been sharpened by recent theory showing that some dopaminergic heterogeneity can be explained by feature-specific prediction errors, in which different neurons compute errors for different aspects of the animal’s state rather than merely different quantiles of one scalar reward variable 8. The most defensible synthesis, then, is that distributional coding and feature-specific coding are complementary rather than mutually exclusive: one concerns asymmetric weighting of outcomes, the other differential weighting of state features, and both may contribute to the observed diversity of dopamine responses 9, 8.

Just as important, the distributional code is likely completed downstream in the striatum through opponent receptor and plasticity machinery. Dopamine’s effects are read out through partially segregated D1- and D2-receptor-expressing spiny projection neuron populations with complementary signaling and plasticity rules, giving the striatum a natural substrate for differentially learning from positive versus negative outcomes 10, 11, 12. Recent work makes that idea much more concrete: Lowet and colleagues found that striatum encodes not only reward mean but reward variance, that chronic dopamine ablation disrupts this distributional representation, and that D1- and D2-expressing neurons preferentially encode opposite tails of the learned reward distribution 13. This suggests that the biological implementation of “distributional RL” is not simply a diverse midbrain population projecting onto a passive striatum; it is a midbrain–striatal composite architecture in which heterogeneous dopaminergic RPE channels are transformed by opponent striatal readout into optimistic and pessimistic learning streams.

The same logic extends from reward magnitude to reward time. At the level of dopamine release in striatal targets, Mohebi, Wei, and colleagues showed that dopamine transients obey a robust ventral-to-dorsolateral gradient of time horizons: dynamics become faster from ventral striatum to dorsomedial striatum to dorsolateral striatum, both in spontaneous fluctuation timescales and in the discounting of future rewards 14. In delay-manipulation experiments, all regions preferred sooner rewards, but DLS discounted delay most steeply whereas VS discounted most shallowly, with DMS intermediate. Computationally, this implies that the effective discount factor in the TD error is not one system-wide constant. Different cortico-basal-ganglia loops appear to receive teaching signals with different implicit γi\gamma_i values, so that limbic loops learn over longer horizons, associative loops over intermediate horizons, and sensorimotor loops over shorter horizons 14, 15. Recent single-neuron work argues that this temporal diversity is not only regional but also cell-specific. Masset, Tano, and colleagues found that individual dopamine neurons encode future rewards over distinct temporal horizons, and that the discount factors inferred from single neurons are correlated across two different behavioral tasks, implying that temporal discounting is a relatively stable property of the neuron rather than a task-by-task reassignment 3. Published in parallel, Sousa, Bujalski, and colleagues extended this logic to a joint code over reward time and magnitude: in their account, each dopamine neuron is characterized by both a temporal parameter (γi\gamma_i) and an asymmetric error-scaling parameter (κi\kappa_i), allowing the population to encode a two-dimensional probabilistic map of future reward over both “when” and “how much” 4. Their results further suggest an efficient-coding organization, in which the distribution of temporal sensitivities adapts to the statistics of experienced delays, and show that reward-time predictions decoded from the dopamine population correlate with anticipatory licking, indicating that this code is behaviorally used rather than epiphenomenal 4.

Overall, the BG error signal is best understood not as one homogeneous scalar broadcast, but as a family of partially specialized teaching signals distributed over reward magnitude and temporal horizon. Mechanistically, that family likely arises from several interacting sources: projection-specific input/output architecture, neuron-to-neuron differences in asymmetric error scaling, topographic specialization of dopamine release across striatal territories, and opponent plasticity rules in dopamine-recipient striatal circuits. At present, however, the field has not converged on a single exhaustive implementation. Some observed heterogeneity may reflect true distributional coding; some may reflect feature-specific errors; some may reflect other task variables layered onto canonical RPE computations. The strongest present claim is therefore not that the classical TD account is wrong, but that it is biologically unfolded: what appears in theory as one scalar δ\delta is implemented in the brain as a structured, heterogeneous population of error signals whose collective action supports risk-sensitive, uncertainty-sensitive, and time-sensitive policy optimization 2, 8, 14, 3, 9.
